opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing to say is that the know-how isn't primarily about volume. People often assume that if you just pour in enough trajectories from enough different robots, the model will figure out what's shared. In practice, the hard part is making data from very different bodies *talk to each other*.

So for me there are a few layers.

The first is the **action representation**. Different robots have different degrees of freedom, different grippers, different control frequencies, some are joint-space, some are end-effector-space. If you just concatenate those raw signals, the model learns robot-specific shortcuts rather than transferable skills. A lot of the real work is designing a shared action space, or at least a consistent mapping, so that "move the hand toward the cup and close" means roughly the same thing whether it's a single-arm tabletop setup or a mobile manipulator. That requires careful normalization, consistent coordinate frames, and alignment of timing. These details sound boring, but they decide whether cross-embodiment transfer works at all.

The second is **data quality and consistency over raw diversity**. Teleoperation data varies enormously depending on the operator, the interface, and how the task was defined. If one dataset has smooth, deliberate demonstrations and another is full of hesitation and corrections, mixing them naively can hurt. So you need filtering, good episode segmentation, and clear task and language annotations, so that the model understands *what* was being attempted, not just how the joints moved.

The third is **balance and mixture**. Some embodiments and tasks are massively overrepresented simply because they're cheap to collect. If you don't reweight, the model becomes very good at a narrow set of setups and weak at generalization. Deciding the mixture ratios, and which sources serve as the "backbone" versus which are for specialization, is quite empirical. You learn it by running a lot of ablations.

And finally, I'd say there's the question of **what non-robot data can contribute**. Human videos, simulation, and web-scale vision-language data don't carry action labels in the same form, but they carry a lot about physics, object affordances, and task structure. Figuring out how to let those sources shape the representation without confusing the action head is, I think, one of the most important open problems right now.

So if I had to sum it up: the core know-how is turning heterogeneous, messy, embodiment-specific experience into something with a shared semantics. The model architecture matters, but the data alignment is where most of the hidden effort goes.

r001.rationale: The response says overrepresented embodiments can dominate and weaken generalization, but it does not state that the model may preferentially use degrees of freedom exercised more often in training.

r002.rationale: It explains that embodiments differ in degrees of freedom, grippers, control frequencies, and action spaces, and calls for normalization and mappings that account for those differences.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the core know-how actually isn't any single trick. It's a mindset about what you're really trying to make the model learn.

When people first hear "cross-embodiment," they imagine the hard part is making data from different robots look similar, so you just normalize everything into a common format and throw it all in. That's the easy part, and it's also mostly wrong as a goal. Different robots have different arms, different grippers, different camera placements, different control frequencies. If you force all of that into one flat representation, you end up either losing information that matters for one embodiment, or confusing the model with signals that mean different things on different bodies. The real question is: what is shared across embodiments, and what isn't?

What's shared is the task structure and the physical common sense. How to approach an object, how to grasp it, what happens when you push something, how to sequence subgoals. What isn't shared is the low-level mapping from that intent to motor commands. So the first piece of know-how is to design the data so the model can separate these two layers. In practice that means being very deliberate about the action space. We spend a lot of time on action representation, whether it's end-effector deltas, joint positions, or something more abstract, and whether it's expressed in a frame that transfers well. A lot of apparent "data problems" turn out to be representation problems.

The second piece is diversity in the right places. People love to quote total hours of data, but hours of nearly identical demonstrations in one lab with one lighting setup are worth very little. What moves the needle is coverage: many objects, many scenes, many ways of doing the same task, and critically, many failure and recovery cases. Human demonstrations tend to be too clean. A model trained only on perfect trajectories doesn't know what to do the moment it drifts off distribution, and in the real world it always drifts. So we deliberately collect data where the operator makes a mistake and recovers, and we treat that as some of the most valuable data we have.

Third is consistency and labeling. When you mix sources, the biggest killer is silent inconsistency. Timestamps that are slightly off between camera and proprioception, calibration that's different from one robot to another, language instructions that describe the same task in ten different granularities. None of this shows up as an obvious error. It just makes the model a little worse everywhere. So a large fraction of the real work is unglamorous: synchronization, calibration, data validation pipelines, and a clear taxonomy for how tasks are described. If I had to name one thing that separates teams who succeed from teams who don't, it's whether they take data hygiene seriously or treat it as someone else's job.

And then there's the question of where the data comes from. Teleoperation is high quality but expensive. Simulation is cheap but has a gap. Human video is almost unlimited but lacks action labels. I don't think any one of them wins. The know-how is in how you combine them: use large, cheap, weakly labeled data to learn visual and semantic priors, and use a smaller amount of high-quality robot data to ground that into actual control. The mixing ratio and the curriculum matter a lot, and honestly that's still more art than science. We run a lot of ablations.

So if I summarize: understand what should transfer and what shouldn't, encode that in your representation, chase diversity rather than volume, be obsessive about consistency, and mix data sources deliberately rather than just pooling them. The models have gotten much better, but the data side is still where most of the real leverage is.

r001.rationale: The response notes that robots can have different control frequencies, but it does not say the model preferentially learns degrees of freedom used more often in training.

r002.rationale: It explains that embodiments differ in arms, grippers, cameras, and controls, and that data representation should account for those differences rather than flattening them into one format.

astra-6.text:
I think the core know-how is deciding what should be shared across robots and what needs to remain specific to each embodiment. Simply pooling data from different robots doesn’t automatically give you useful transfer.

For example, two demonstrations might both show a robot picking up a cup, but the camera views, joint configurations, control frequencies, and action representations can be very different. You need to align observations and actions so the model can learn the common task structure without losing the physical constraints of each robot. Even something as basic as whether an action is expressed in the camera frame or the robot’s base frame matters a lot.

Then there’s data quality and balance. A large dataset from one robot can dominate training, while a smaller dataset from another robot might contain the behaviors you actually need. So filtering, synchronization, task annotation, and sampling are all part of the recipe.

Ultimately, I’d judge that recipe by transfer: does adding data from another embodiment help the target robot learn a task with less data? That feedback loop—prepare the data, train, test on the robot, and identify what’s missing—is where much of the practical know-how lives.

r001.rationale: The response discusses dataset imbalance, but does not state that a model may preferentially learn degrees of freedom exercised more often in training.

r002.rationale: It says data must account for embodiment-specific differences, including camera views, joint configurations, control frequencies, action representations, and physical constraints.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the core know-how is deciding what should be shared across embodiments and what needs to remain specific to each robot. Simply pooling more trajectories is not enough. Different robots have different joints, grippers, camera views, and control frequencies, so the same task can look very different in the raw data.

You need a consistent way to represent observations, actions, and task intent, while preserving enough information about the embodiment for the model to interpret them correctly. For example, an end-effector motion command needs a clearly defined coordinate frame and timing. Otherwise, two datasets can appear compatible while actually teaching conflicting behaviors.

Then there’s data quality and balance: checking synchronization, understanding failures, and making sure one robot or one easy task doesn’t dominate training. The real test is whether adding data from another embodiment improves performance on the target robot. That feedback is what tells you whether your data preparation is creating useful transfer.

r001.rationale: The response mentions balancing data across robots and tasks, but does not state that a model may preferentially learn degrees of freedom exercised more frequently in training.

r002.rationale: It says preparation must distinguish what is shared from what remains specific to each robot and preserve embodiment information, citing differences in joints, grippers, camera views, and control frequencies.
